notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

This section is about tools and the order to use them in. One idea runs through it: every hop has its own view of a request, and the hop that generated a symptom knows why.

  • curl, dig, nc and ss each ask one layer one precise question.
  • The browser and traces show what the server-side tools can't.
  • Metrics locate the hop; playbooks give the order of checks.

The skill is choosing the question that rules out the most suspects first.

Concept map

Layer tools first, then the views that span hops, then the playbooks that combine them.

Green is CORE, blue is SUPPORTING; 160–161 and 165–166 each group two SUPPORTING notes. Item 163 (packet capture) is a BREADTH card in breadth. Neighbours: where latency goes owns the curl -w arithmetic these tools feed, and streaming LLM tokens applies the playbooks to AI traffic.

Reading order:curlDNS toolspath and reachabilitysocket statepacket capturebrowser Network paneltracingmetricstriage playbooks

The order follows the layers a request crosses: name, path, connection, wire, then the views that span hops. Playbooks come last because they use every tool before them.

Owners

Each idea is explained in full in one note. Other notes link to it and don't repeat it.

Idea Owner note

Decision trees

Can't reach a service. Which tool first? Ask in this order. The first "no" decides.

Which symptom points where?

Symptom First check Owner
half the team sees the old IP TTL and aa in dig 160
ping fails, service may be fine nc -vz host port 161
service stops accepting after days CLOSE_WAIT count 162
curl fine, users see errors DevTools: preflight, cookies, queueing 164
trace has a gap which hop dropped traceparent 165
LB p99 ≫ service p99 pool saturation between them 166

The direction is consistent: from one tool per layer, run by hand, to one ID and one metric schema that follow a request across every hop.

Before you leave

  • One big idea: ask the hop that generated the symptom, with the tool for that layer.
  • Two most-confused pairs: refused vs timed out (the host answered vs the path dropped), and 502 vs 504 (upstream refused vs slower than the proxy's timeout).
  • Ten minutes before a tech discussion: say "--resolve keeps SNI"; say "CLOSE_WAIT is ours"; say "6 per host on HTTP/1.1"; say "percentiles don't average"; walk the 5xx tree in 167.
  • Across sections: the playbooks lean on timeouts and outlier detection; AI traffic meets them in streaming LLM tokens.

headings.text: Packet capture: tcpdump, and when you need Wireshark

notes.html:
One tool you reach for only after the others have narrowed the question: when curl, socket state and traces disagree about what was actually on the wire.

Packet capture: tcpdump, and when you need Wireshark

Stage: frame · per packet

tcpdump records packets on a host. Capture to a file with a tight filter: tcpdump -i any -nn -s0 -w cap.pcap 'host 10.0.1.7 and port 443' (-nn stops it making its own DNS lookups). It settles who sent the RST, whether the SYN left, and the gap between request and first byte. TLS hides bodies unless the client writes SSLKEYLOGFILE; handshake, SNI, sizes and timing stay visible. Wireshark adds stream following and retransmission analysis. Captures hold real data: delete them after use. In Kubernetes, capture from an ephemeral container via kubectl debug. Related: retransmission.

notes.title: curl Mastery — Pin the Backend, Force the Protocol, Read -v Honestly
notes.html:
References

curl man page · everything.curl.dev: --resolve and --connect-to · everything.curl.dev: write-out variables · everything.curl.dev: HTTP versions

TL;DR

curl is the one HTTP client on every machine, and five habits make it a precise instrument:

  • -w splits time into segments (where latency goes owns the arithmetic).
  • --resolve host:port:IP sends a request to one chosen backend while keeping the real hostname for SNI, certificate checks and Host. Overriding only -H 'Host:' breaks TLS.
  • -v shows what was negotiated: the IP connected to, TLS version, ALPN (h2 or http/1.1), and the exact request and response headers.
  • -I, not -X HEAD: -X changes the method word but not curl's behaviour, so it waits for a body that never comes.
  • Force versions (--http1.1, --http2, --http3, --tlsv1.2 --tls-max 1.2) to test what clients will actually negotiate.

curl isn't a browser: no Origin, cookies, preflight or connection limits. "Works in curl" rules out the server, not the browser path.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:suspect one backend--resolve pins it, SNI intact-v shows IP, TLS, ALPN, headers-w splits the timeforce a protocol or TLS version to comparerepeat from where the caller runs

Recall

Prompt Answer
Hit one backend without editing /etc/hosts? --resolve api.example.com:443:10.0.1.7: SNI and Host stay correct.
Why not just -H 'Host: api.example.com' against the IP? SNI and the certificate check use the URL's host, so TLS fails or hits the wrong vhost.
-I vs -X HEAD? -I sends HEAD and expects no body; -X HEAD waits for one until timeout.
Where does -v show ALPN? * ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1 and the server's choice on the next lines.
Why does curl succeed where the browser fails? No Origin, cookies, CORS preflight or CSP: the browser path is different.
Draw by hand: --resolve DNS box crossed out; arrow from curl straight to 10.0.1.7; inside the TLS ClientHello write "SNI = api.example.com"; inside the request write "Host: api.example.com".

The idea

One of six backends behind a load balancer returns stale data. Through the LB, curl https://api.example.com hits a random one each time. Someone runs curl -H 'Host: api.example.com' https://10.0.1.7/ and gets a certificate error, because curl sent SNI and checked the certificate for 10.0.1.7. They add -k to skip verification, and now they're testing a request no real client sends.

curl --resolve api.example.com:443:10.0.1.7 https://api.example.com/ connects to that one backend and sends exactly what a client would: real SNI, real certificate check, real Host.

The trade: curl reproduces a server-side exchange exactly and scriptably, and you pay by having to know which flags change what's on the wire, and by remembering it is not a browser.

How it works

What each flag changes on the wire.

Flag Changes Leaves alone Use it for
--resolve h:p:IP where curl connects SNI, cert check, Host one backend behind an LB or CDN
--connect-to h:p:h2:p2 where curl connects, by name SNI, cert check, Host routing to another hostname
-H 'Host: …' the Host header only SNI and cert check (still the URL host) plain HTTP vhosts only
-I method HEAD, expects no body everything else headers only
-X METHOD the method word only how curl reads the response PUT, DELETE with a body
--http2, --http3, --http1.1 ALPN offer the request what will clients negotiate?
--tlsv1.2 --tls-max 1.2 the TLS version range the request old-client compatibility
-k skips certificate checks never in a real diagnosis

Evolution

Lineage:1998 curl 4.0Dec 2010 --resolve (7.21.3)2016 --connect-to (7.49.0)Oct 2018 HTTP/2 the default for HTTPS (7.62.0)2022 --http3 usable in builds with a QUIC library
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: curl 8 adds time_posttransfer and time_queue; HTTP/3 works in builds with a QUIC library (macOS's system curl is built without it).
  • What won't change: SNI comes from the URL host, not the Host header.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (curl 8.7.1 on macOS; a Python 3.15 HTTPS server with a certificate for api.example.test):

curl -s --cacert c.pem https://api.example.test:8443/health -w '%{http_code}\n'
# 000, exit 6                       ← no DNS record for the name: can't resolve
curl -s --cacert c.pem --resolve api.example.test:8443:127.0.0.1 https://api.example.test:8443/health \
  -w '  http %{http_code} ip %{remote_ip}\n'
# {"ok":true}  http 200 ip 127.0.0.1
curl -sv … -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Added|Connected|SSL connection|ALPN|^> (GET|Host)|^< HTTP'
# * Added api.example.test:8443:127.0.0.1 to DNS cache
# * Connected to api.example.test (127.0.0.1) port 8443
# * ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1
# * SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / AEAD-AES256-GCM-SHA384
# * ALPN: server did not agree on a protocol. Uses default.     ← so this is HTTP/1.1, not h2
# > GET /health HTTP/1.1
# > Host: api.example.test:8443
# < HTTP/1.1 200 OK
curl -sI …                -w 'time %{time_total}\n'    # time 0.001046
curl -s -X HEAD --max-time 3 … -w 'time %{time_total}'  # time 3.006141, exit 28   ← waited for a body
curl -s --tlsv1.2 --tls-max 1.2 … -w '%{http_code}\n'   # 200   ← the server still accepts TLS 1.2

The default that bites: without --max-time, curl has no total timeout, so -X HEAD (or a stuck server) hangs indefinitely.

Break it: a model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026) against the same server: the -H Host approach vs --resolve, written as raw TLS.

def get(connect_to, sni, host_header):
    s = ctx.wrap_socket(socket.create_connection((connect_to, 8443)), server_hostname=sni)
    s.sendall(f"GET /health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host_header}\r\n\r\n".encode())
get("127.0.0.1", "127.0.0.1", "api.example.test")          # what -H 'Host:' against the IP does
get("127.0.0.1", "api.example.test", "api.example.test")   # what --resolve does
# look for: the TLS step
# naive belief predicts: setting the Host header is enough to reach the right site

Run: the Host-only request failed before HTTP with "IP address mismatch, certificate is not valid for '127.0.0.1'"; the --resolve form returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Measure it

  • See it: -v for what was negotiated, -w '%{remote_ip} %{http_version} %{ssl_verify_result}' for one-line proof, --trace-ascii - for every byte.
  • In production: run the same curl --resolve against each backend IP from a host in the caller's network; a scheduled synthetic check with -w timings per backend.
  • Bounded by: curl isn't a browser → browser Network panel; segment arithmetic → where latency goes.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I use curl as a precise client. --resolve pins one backend while keeping SNI and Host real; -v shows the IP, TLS version, ALPN and headers; -w splits time into DNS, connect, TLS and wait; and I force HTTP or TLS versions to see what clients negotiate. I use -I, never -X HEAD, always --max-time, never -k. And I remember it's not a browser, so CORS and cookie issues won't show.

Q · Mechanism — Why does --resolve keep TLS working when -H Host doesn't? TLS starts before HTTP. The ClientHello's SNI and the certificate check both use the hostname from the URL. --resolve changes only which IP that hostname maps to inside curl, so SNI and certificate checks still use the real name. -H Host only rewrites the HTTP header after TLS, which by then has already used the IP.

Q · Trade-off — --resolve or --connect-to? --resolve maps a name to an IP: simple, and right for "this backend IP". --connect-to maps a host and port to another host and port, which still gets resolved: right for "send api.example.com traffic to staging-lb.internal". Both keep SNI and Host. IP-level work: --resolve; name-level redirection: --connect-to.

Q · Failure — curl gets 200 from the CDN but users see 403. What's going on? The browser sends things curl doesn't: Origin, cookies, a preflight OPTIONS, a different User-Agent, maybe HTTP/3. A WAF or CORS rule keys on one of them. Replay the browser's request with "Copy as cURL" from DevTools, then remove headers one by one until it passes.

Q · Design — A synthetic check that catches one bad backend behind an LB.

  • Per backend: curl --resolve against each target IP from the target group, with real SNI.
  • Record: -w timings, %{http_version}, %{ssl_verify_result}, status and a response checksum.
  • Alert: on any backend that differs from the rest, not only on errors.
  • Run from: each caller region, every minute.

Compare

curl Browser Language HTTP client
Sends Origin, cookies, preflight no yes only if coded
Connection limits per host none 6 for HTTP/1.1 pool settings
Pins a backend --resolve no custom resolver
Best for server-side behaviour user-visible behaviour what your service actually does

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
-X HEAD with --max-time 3 3.006 s, exit 28 waits for a body measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
-I 0.001 s same server measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
curl exit codes worth knowing 6 resolve, 7 connect, 28 timeout, 35 TLS, 60 cert first thing to read spec (as of Nov 2026): curl man page
curl default total timeout none set --max-time default (as of Nov 2026): curl man page

Pitfalls

  • "-H 'Host: name' against the IP tests that site"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it worked for plain HTTP vhosts for decades.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: over HTTPS, SNI and the certificate check use the URL host, so you fail TLS or hit the default vhost.
    ↳ Think instead: --resolve name:443:IP and keep the real URL.
  • Don't reach for -k to "get past" a certificate error.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it makes the error go away immediately.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the certificate problem is often the bug, and every real client still sees it.
    ↳ Do instead: read the error, check SNI with -v, pass the right CA with --cacert.
  • "-X HEAD is the same as -I"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: both put HEAD on the request line.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: -X changes only the method word; curl still expects a body and waits until timeout.
    ↳ Think instead: -I for HEAD; -X only for methods with normal bodies.
  • Not the same: works in curl vs works for users
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are HTTP requests to the same URL.
    ↳ Difference: browsers add Origin, cookies, preflights, connection limits and often HTTP/3.
    ↳ Think instead: "Copy as cURL" from DevTools to replay the real request.
  • Don't run curl without --max-time in scripts.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: interactive runs finish fine.
    ↳ What goes wrong: curl has no total timeout by default, so a stuck server hangs the check or the CI job forever.
    ↳ Do instead: --connect-timeout 2 --max-time 10 on every scripted call.
  • Shelf life: --resolve, -v and SNI rules are durable; HTTP/3 support and new -w variables move.

Connections

Path:where latency goescurl masteryDNS toolstriage playbooks
  • Builds on the TLS 1.3 handshake (SNI) and when each HTTP version matters.
  • Owned elsewhere: where latency goes owns -w segment math; CORS owns the browser-only failures.
  • Breaks when combined with -k, which hides the certificate bug you came to find.
  • Bounded by being one client from one place: it shows the server, not every user's path.

notes.title: DNS Tools — dig, +trace, and Reading an Answer Honestly
notes.html:
References

dig(1) man page (BIND 9) · RFC 1035 §4.1.1: header flags · RFC 2308: negative caching · RFC 8914: extended DNS errors

TL;DR

dig shows a DNS answer and how it was obtained. Four things to read every time:

  • Status: NOERROR, NXDOMAIN (the name doesn't exist) or SERVFAIL (the resolver couldn't get an answer).
  • Flags: aa means an authoritative server answered; its absence means a cache did. ra means recursion is available.
  • TTL: a number lower than the configured one means you're seeing a cached copy, counting down.
  • ANSWER count: NOERROR with zero answers means the name exists but has no records of that type, which is different from NXDOMAIN.

@server asks a specific server; +trace walks from the root yourself, bypassing your resolver's cache.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:dig name (what my resolver says, maybe cached)dig @authoritative name (what the owner says, aa)compare TTL and datadig +trace name (walk the delegation)the hop that disagrees is the bug

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which flag says the answer came from the authority? aa; without it, a cache answered.
NXDOMAIN vs NOERROR with ANSWER 0? The name doesn't exist vs the name exists, but not for that type.
What does +trace bypass? Your recursive resolver and its cache: it queries root, TLD, then authoritative servers itself.

The idea

After a DNS change, half the team sees the new IP and half the old. dig api.example.com on one laptop shows the old address with TTL 1,742. That number is the clue: the record's TTL was 3,600, so this resolver cached it 31 minutes ago and will keep serving it for 29 more. dig @ns1.provider.net api.example.com returns the new IP with aa set. Nothing is broken; caches are doing their job until the TTL runs out.

The trade: DNS caching makes resolution fast and resilient, and you pay with answers that differ by where you ask and when, so every DNS debugging session starts by asking who answered.

How it works

Field in the output Meaning Tells you
status: NOERROR + ANSWER ≥ 1 records found normal
status: NOERROR + ANSWER 0 name exists, no records of this type wrong type, or a missing record (often AAAA)
status: NXDOMAIN the name doesn't exist typo, missing record, or wrong zone (private vs public)
status: SERVFAIL the resolver couldn't get an answer broken delegation, DNSSEC failure, authority down
flags: aa authoritative answer the source of truth
flags: ra without aa a recursive resolver answered from cache or recursion maybe stale
TTL below the configured value time left in someone's cache how long until it changes

Evolution

Lineage:1987 DNS (RFC 1034/1035)1990s nslookup1998 negative caching (RFC 2308)2000 dig in BIND 92020 extended DNS errors (RFC 8914)2020s kdig and doggo for DoT and DoH
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: resolvers return extended errors (EDE) explaining SERVFAIL; macOS still ships dig 9.10.6.
  • What won't change: cached answers count down; aa marks the source.

On the wire

Captured 24 Nov 2026 with dig 9.10.6 on macOS (reserved example domains):

dig example.com A +noall +answer +comments
# status: NOERROR
# flags: qr rd ra ad; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2      ← no aa: my resolver answered; ad: DNSSEC validated
# example.com.   229   IN   A   104.20.23.154    ← 229 s left in its cache
dig example.org CAA +noall +comments            # status: NOERROR, ANSWER: 0   ← name exists, no CAA records
dig nxdomain-check.invalid A +noall +comments   # status: NXDOMAIN             ← name doesn't exist
dig example.com A +norecurse @a.iana-servers.net
# flags: qr aa; ANSWER: 6                       ← aa: the authority answered

The default that bites: nslookup and getent hide flags and TTLs, and dig without @ asks your configured resolver, which may be a corporate or VPN one that answers private names differently.

Measure it

  • See it: the same query against your resolver, a public resolver and the authoritative server: three answers tell you who's stale.
  • In production: resolver SERVFAIL and NXDOMAIN rates, query latency p99, and a synthetic dig @authoritative check after every change.
  • Bounded by: caches → TTL and caching layers; in-cluster search lists → CoreDNS.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I read four things in every dig output: status, the aa flag, the TTL and the answer count. No aa and a reduced TTL means a cache answered; NXDOMAIN means the name doesn't exist, while NOERROR with no answers means the type is missing. Then I ask the authoritative server directly with @, and use +trace to walk the delegation when they disagree.

Q · Mechanism — What does +trace actually do? It starts at a root server, asks for the name without recursion, follows the referral to the TLD servers, then to the zone's authoritative servers, printing each step. It doesn't use your resolver's cache, so it shows what a fresh lookup would get, and which delegation step is broken.

Q · Trade-off — Lower TTLs before a migration, or keep them long? Low TTLs make a cutover propagate in minutes but raise query volume and make you more exposed to a DNS provider outage. Long TTLs are resilient but slow to change. Lower the TTL a full old-TTL period before the change, cut over, then raise it again.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Captured cached TTL 229 s example.com A from my resolver measured, 24 Nov 2026
DNS response codes worth knowing NOERROR 0, SERVFAIL 2, NXDOMAIN 3, REFUSED 5 header RCODE spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 1035
Negative-cache TTL from the SOA minimum how long NXDOMAIN sticks spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 2308

Pitfalls

  • "dig shows what DNS says"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it prints a clean answer with no caveats.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it shows what one resolver says right now, often from cache, and private zones answer differently by network.
    ↳ Think instead: check aa, the TTL and which server answered.
  • Not the same: NXDOMAIN vs NOERROR with no answer
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "no address came back".
    ↳ Difference: NXDOMAIN says the name doesn't exist at all; NOERROR/0 says it exists but lacks that record type.
    ↳ Think instead: read the status line before the answer section.
  • Don't create the record after clients have already asked for it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: create records just before launch.
    ↳ What goes wrong: early lookups cached NXDOMAIN for the SOA's negative TTL, so the new record stays invisible for a while.
    ↳ Do instead: create records before anything queries them, or check the SOA minimum.
  • "SERVFAIL means the record is wrong"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's an error about that name.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it means the resolver couldn't complete the lookup: broken delegation, unreachable authorities or a DNSSEC failure.
    ↳ Think instead: +trace and +cd to find which step fails.
  • Shelf life: flags, status codes and TTL behaviour are durable; tools for DoH and DoT move.

Connections

Path:curl masteryDNS toolspath and reachability
  • Builds on DNS resolution and record types.
  • Owned elsewhere: DNS as an outage cause owns failure patterns.
  • Breaks when combined with a VPN or split-horizon resolver you forgot you're using.
  • Bounded by caches you can't see: the user's resolver may differ from yours.

notes.title: Path & Reachability — Refused, Timed Out, or Open: Proving a Port
notes.html:
References

nc(1) man page (OpenBSD netcat) · mtr documentation · traceroute(8) man page · RIPE Labs: Interpreting traceroute

TL;DR

"Can I reach it?" has three different answers, and each points somewhere else:

  • Open: the TCP handshake completes in about 1 RTT. The port is reachable and something is listening.
  • Refused: an immediate reset. The host is reachable but nothing listens on that port (or a firewall rejects).
  • Timed out: silence. Something on the path drops packets: a security group, NACL, firewall or missing route.

nc -vz host port tells them apart in one command. ping only tests ICMP, which is often blocked while TCP works. traceroute and mtr show the path, but loss at a middle hop that doesn't continue to the end is just a router deprioritising ICMP.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:nc -vz host 443succeeded: reachable, listeningrefused: reachable, nothing listeningtimed out: dropped on the pathmtr or traceroute -T -p 443 to see wherecheck SG, NACL, routes at that point

Recall

Prompt Answer
Refused vs timed out? Refused: host answered with a reset. Timed out: something dropped the packets.
Why can ping fail while the service works? ICMP is blocked or rate-limited; TCP isn't.
100 % loss at hop 6 but the destination answers? That router doesn't answer TTL-exceeded probes; it's not forwarding loss.

The idea

A service can't reach a new database. ping fails, so the team blames the network and opens a ticket. nc -vz db 5432 returns "Connection refused" instantly: the network is fine, the host answered, and Postgres isn't listening on that interface (listen_addresses = 'localhost'). The ping failed only because the security group doesn't allow ICMP. Ten seconds with the right tool saves a day of waiting on the wrong team.

The trade: a TCP probe answers reachability precisely and safely, and you pay with remembering that each tool tests a different thing, so a failed ping or a lossy middle hop proves almost nothing.

How it works

Result of nc -vz host port Time What happened Look at
succeeded ~1 RTT SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK it's not the network; check TLS and the app
connection refused ~1 RTT SYN answered by RST the process, its bind address, or a REJECT rule
timed out your -G/-w limit SYN never answered security groups, NACLs, firewalls, routes
no route to host immediate local routing or ICMP unreachable the client's route table 
traceroute -T -p 443 host    ← TCP SYN probes on the real port, so firewalls treat them like real traffic
mtr -T -P 443 host           ← the same, sampled continuously: per-hop loss and latency over time

Evolution

Lineage:1983 ping1988 traceroute (Van Jacobson)1995 netcat1997 mtr2000s TCP traceroute (-T) for firewalled paths2020s VPC Reachability Analyzer and similar path analysers
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: cloud path analysers compute reachability from config without sending packets.
  • What won't change: a reset and a silence mean different things.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (macOS nc; port 8443 had a listener, 8444 didn't; 10.255.255.1 is a non-routed address that drops everything):

nc -vz 127.0.0.1 8443          # Connection to 127.0.0.1 port 8443 [tcp/pcsync-https] succeeded!
nc -vz 127.0.0.1 8444          # nc: connectx to 127.0.0.1 port 8444 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
time nc -vz -G 3 10.255.255.1 443
# nc: connectx to 10.255.255.1 port 443 (tcp) failed: Operation timed out
# 3.008 total                  ← it waited the full 3 s: silence, not a refusal

The default that bites: without -G (macOS) or -w (Linux), nc waits for the kernel's SYN retries, about 75 s on macOS and over 2 minutes on Linux.

Measure it

  • See it: nc -vz from the caller's subnet, not your laptop; traceroute -T -p <port> when it times out.
  • In production: VPC flow logs with REJECT for the pair, a reachability analyser query, and synthetic TCP checks between tiers.
  • Bounded by: the filters themselves → security groups vs NACLs; routes → route tables.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I test the real port with TCP, nc -vz host port, from where the caller runs. Succeeded means reachable and listening; refused means the host answered but nothing listens; timed out means something dropped the packets, so I look at security groups, NACLs and routes. I don't trust ping, which tests ICMP, and I ignore loss at middle traceroute hops unless it continues to the end.

Q · Mechanism — Why does loss at a middle hop in traceroute often mean nothing? Traceroute gets each hop's reply from the router's own control plane, which rate-limits or deprioritises ICMP TTL-exceeded messages. Forwarding happens in hardware and isn't affected. If hop 6 shows 60 % loss but hops 7 to the end show 0 %, packets are getting through; only hop 6's replies are lost.

Q · Trade-off — Active probes or flow logs? Probes (nc, mtr) give an immediate answer for one pair but only test from where you run them. Flow logs show every real flow and whether it was accepted, after a delay of minutes. Probe to confirm a hypothesis now; flow logs to find which pairs are failing across the fleet.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Timed-out probe with -G 3 3.008 s silence until the limit measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Refused immediate RST from the host measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Linux default SYN retries 6 (about 127 s) net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries default (as of Nov 2026): Linux ip-sysctl docs

Pitfalls

  • "Ping fails, so the host is unreachable"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: ping is the first tool everyone learns.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: ICMP is often blocked by security groups or firewalls while the TCP port works fine.
    ↳ Think instead: test the real port with TCP.
  • Not the same: refused vs timed out
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "couldn't connect".
    ↳ Difference: refused means the host replied with a reset (the app or its bind address); timed out means packets were dropped on the path.
    ↳ Think instead: reset → host owner; silence → network owner.
  • Don't test from your laptop and conclude for the service.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the fastest place to type the command.
    ↳ What goes wrong: your path, VPN and source IP differ from the caller's, so you test different rules.
    ↳ Do instead: run the probe from the caller's subnet, or an instance with the caller's security group.
  • "Mid-path loss in traceroute is the problem"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the red percentage stands out on screen.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: routers deprioritise replies to probes; loss that stops at the next hop isn't forwarding loss.
    ↳ Think instead: only loss that continues to the destination counts.
  • Shelf life: the three TCP outcomes are permanent; cloud path tools move.

Connections

Path:DNS toolspath and reachabilitysocket state
  • Builds on the three-way handshake and routing basics.
  • Owned elsewhere: security groups vs NACLs owns why packets are dropped.
  • Breaks when combined with an ICMP-blocking policy and a habit of using ping.
  • Bounded by where you probe from: a test proves one path only.

notes.title: Socket State — ss, and What Each TCP State Is Accusing
notes.html:
References

ss(8) man page · RFC 9293 §3.3.2: TCP state machine · Cloudflare blog: This is strictly a violation of the TCP specification (CLOSE_WAIT) · netstat(1), macOS

TL;DR

Counting sockets by TCP state points at a specific bug:

  • CLOSE_WAIT piling up: your application's bug. The peer closed, your code never called close(). It's a leak.
  • TIME_WAIT piling up: the side that closed first; normal, but on a client it eats ephemeral ports. Pool your connections.
  • SYN-SENT stuck: packets to the peer are being dropped (a firewall or route).
  • SYN-RECV piling up: your accept queue or SYN backlog is full, or a SYN flood.
  • LISTEN with Recv-Q near Send-Q: the accept queue is full and new connections are dropped.

ss -tan state close-wait on Linux (netstat -an on macOS) is the whole investigation.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:ss -s for totalsss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c by statethe dominant state names the suspectss -tanp state close-wait names the processfix code or pooling

Recall

Prompt Answer
Thousands of CLOSE_WAIT: whose bug? Yours: the peer sent FIN, your code never closed.
Thousands of TIME_WAIT: whose bug? Usually none; it's the side that closed first. On a client, pool to save ports.
Recv-Q on a LISTEN socket? Connections waiting to be accepted; Send-Q is the backlog limit.

The idea

A service slowly stops accepting requests over days and is "fixed" by restarts. ss -tan state close-wait | wc -l shows 28,000. Every one is a connection the upstream closed while the service held on to it: an HTTP client response body never read and closed on an error path. Each leaked socket holds a file descriptor, and at the ulimit the process can't open anything new. The network was never involved.

The trade: the kernel already tracks every connection's state for free, and you pay only with learning what each state accuses, after which most "network" problems turn out to be one line of code.

How it works

The close sequence, and where each state appears.

State piling up Means Owner
CLOSE_WAIT peer closed, app hasn't your code: an unclosed socket or response body
FIN_WAIT_2 we closed, peer hasn't the peer's code (its CLOSE_WAIT)
TIME_WAIT we closed first, waiting 60 s nobody; pool connections if ports run low
SYN-SENT our SYN unanswered the path: firewall, SG, route
SYN-RECV handshake half done on our side accept backlog, SYN flood

Evolution

Lineage:1981 TCP state machine (RFC 793)1980s netstat2001 ss in iproute22022 RFC 9293 consolidates TCP2020s eBPF tools (tcplife, tcpstates) trace transitions live
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: eBPF tools show which process moved which socket between states, and when.
  • What won't change: CLOSE_WAIT belongs to whoever hasn't called close().

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (macOS netstat; a Python 3.15 server on port 9101 that accepted three connections and never closed them, closed two others itself, and kept one open):

netstat -an -p tcp | grep '\.9101'
# 127.0.0.1.9101  127.0.0.1.51873  CLOSE_WAIT     ← client closed; server never called close()
# 127.0.0.1.51873 127.0.0.1.9101   FIN_WAIT_2     ← the client's side of the same leak
# … two more CLOSE_WAIT / FIN_WAIT_2 pairs
# 127.0.0.1.9101  127.0.0.1.51874  TIME_WAIT      ← server closed first, so the server holds TIME_WAIT
# 127.0.0.1.9101  127.0.0.1.51876  ESTABLISHED    ← the healthy pair
# 127.0.0.1.9101  *.*              LISTEN

On Linux the same view is ss -tanp (with -p for the owning process). The default that bites: netstat is deprecated on Linux and slow on busy hosts; ss -s gives totals instantly.

Measure it

  • See it: ss -tan | awk 'NR>1{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c; ss -ltn for Recv-Q/Send-Q on listeners.
  • In production: sockets by state per process (node exporter node_sockstat_*, node_netstat_TcpExt_ListenOverflows), open file descriptors vs the limit.
  • Bounded by: port exhaustion → pooling; teardown → connection teardown.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I count sockets by state, because each state accuses someone. CLOSE_WAIT means our code didn't close after the peer did: a leak. TIME_WAIT is the side that closed first; normal, but it eats ports on clients, so pool. SYN-SENT stuck means packets are dropped on the path. A listener with Recv-Q near its backlog means we're dropping new connections. ss with -p names the process.

Q · Mechanism — Why does CLOSE_WAIT never time out by itself? The peer sent FIN, so the kernel moved the socket to CLOSE_WAIT and is waiting for the application to call close(). TCP has no timer for that state; the kernel can't know whether the app still wants to send. It stays until the process closes the descriptor or exits.

Q · Trade-off — Tune TIME_WAIT away or pool connections? Kernel tweaks (tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing connections) let a client reuse TIME_WAIT ports sooner, but treat the symptom. Pooling removes the churn that created them, plus the handshakes. Pool first; tcp_tw_reuse only for clients that must open many short connections.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Linux TIME_WAIT 60 s fixed TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN default (as of Nov 2026): Linux kernel
CLOSE_WAIT timeout none until close() spec (as of Nov 2026): RFC 9293
Captured leak 3 CLOSE_WAIT, 3 FIN_WAIT_2 server never closed measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Default somaxconn 4,096 (Linux ≥ 5.4) accept-queue cap default (as of Nov 2026): Linux ip-sysctl docs

Pitfalls

  • "CLOSE_WAIT is a network problem"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a TCP state, shown by network tools.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the network delivered the FIN correctly; only the application can leave this state, by closing.
    ↳ Think instead: find the code path that doesn't close, often an error path.
  • Don't "fix" TIME_WAIT with tcp_tw_recycle.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: old blog posts recommend it for port exhaustion.
    ↳ What goes wrong: it dropped connections from clients behind NAT, and it was removed from Linux in 4.12.
    ↳ Do instead: pool connections; tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing only.
  • Not the same: CLOSE_WAIT vs FIN_WAIT_2
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: they're the two halves of the same half-closed connection, and both look stuck.
    ↳ Difference: CLOSE_WAIT is on the side that hasn't closed; FIN_WAIT_2 is on the side waiting for it.
    ↳ Think instead: the CLOSE_WAIT side owns the bug.
  • "A listener's Recv-Q is unread data"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: on connected sockets, it is.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: on LISTEN it's the number of completed connections waiting for accept(); near the backlog, new ones are dropped.
    ↳ Think instead: listener Recv-Q = accept backlog in use.
  • Shelf life: the state meanings are permanent; tooling (ss, eBPF) moves.

Connections

Path:path and reachabilitysocket statepacket capturetriage playbooks
  • Builds on connection teardown and sockets and ports.
  • Owned elsewhere: pooling owns TIME_WAIT port exhaustion.
  • Breaks when combined with error paths that skip closing response bodies.
  • Bounded by the file-descriptor limit: every leaked socket holds one.

notes.title: The Browser Network Panel — Queueing, Protocol and Preflight: What curl Can't Show
notes.html:
References

Chrome DevTools: Network features reference · Chrome DevTools: Timing breakdown · MDN: Resource Timing · MDN: CORS preflight

TL;DR

The browser is the client your users run, and it behaves differently from curl:

  • Queueing: HTTP/1.1 allows 6 connections per host, so the seventh request waits inside the browser. DevTools shows it as Queueing or Stalled.
  • Protocol: each request may use http/1.1, h2 or h3. The Protocol column (hidden by default) shows which.
  • Extra requests: CORS preflights (OPTIONS), cookies, redirects and cache hits ((disk cache), (memory cache)).

The timing breakdown per request (Queueing, Stalled, DNS, Initial connection, SSL, Request sent, Waiting for server response, Content download) maps onto curl -w segments, plus the time spent inside the browser before anything left it. "Copy as cURL" turns any row into a reproducible command.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:open Network panel, disable cachereloadsort by Waterfalllong grey Queueing bar? connection limitlong green Waiting? serverOPTIONS row before a request? preflightProtocol column says which HTTP versionCopy as cURL to reproduce

Recall

Prompt Answer
Long Queueing or Stalled bar? The request hadn't left the browser: connection limit or waiting for a socket.
Which column proves h2? Protocol: hidden by default, enable it from the column menu.
A request preceded by an OPTIONS? A CORS preflight, which curl never sends.

The idea

A dashboard loads 30 small API calls over HTTP/1.1 and takes 5 seconds, though each call takes 1 second on the server and they all start at once. The waterfall shows the shape: six bars start together, then six more start a second later, then six more. The browser opens at most 6 connections to one host, so 30 requests take 5 rounds. curl in a loop shows "1 second each" and misses all of it. Serving the API over HTTP/2 puts all 30 on one connection in parallel.

The trade: the browser applies real-world limits (connections, CORS, caching) that keep the web safe and fair, and you pay by having to diagnose user-visible slowness in the browser itself, because server-side tools can't see those limits.

How it works

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (Chrome; a Python 3.15 HTTP/1.1 server whose /slow waits 1 s; the page fired 12 fetch calls at once and read their Resource Timing entries):

Requests Protocol Queued in the browser Waiting for server Total
0–5 http/1.1 8–10 ms ~1,005 ms ~1,017 ms
6–11 http/1.1 ~1,017 ms ~1,005 ms ~2,023 ms

Six went out at once; the other six waited a full second inside the browser for a free connection.

DevTools phase Means curl -w equivalent
Queueing / Stalled waiting inside the browser none
DNS Lookup name resolution time_namelookup
Initial connection, SSL TCP and TLS connect, appconnect
Waiting for server response 1 RTT + server time starttransfer − pretransfer
Content Download body transfer total − starttransfer

Evolution

Lineage:2006 Firebug's Net panel2009 WebKit Web Inspector network timeline2012 Resource Timing API2015 HTTP/2 in browsers ends the 6-connection workaround2020s HTTP/3 shown as h3, and Chrome's override and throttling tools
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: DevTools shows early hints, server timing and the reason a request was blocked; HTTP/3 shows as h3.
  • What won't change: the browser adds limits and requests no server-side tool reproduces.

On the wire

Reading the same data from code, as the capture above did:

performance.getEntriesByType("resource").map(e => ({
  proto: e.nextHopProtocol,                         // "http/1.1", "h2", "h3"
  queued_ms: e.requestStart - e.startTime,          // time inside the browser before sending
  wait_ms: e.responseStart - e.requestStart,        // 1 RTT + server time
}))
// the default that bites: cross-origin entries show zeros for the breakdown
// unless the response sends Timing-Allow-Origin

Measure it

  • See it: DevTools Network with cache disabled and the Protocol column on; throttling presets to see slow-network behaviour; "Copy as cURL" to reproduce one row.
  • In production: Real User Monitoring of Resource Timing and Navigation Timing (queued time, protocol, TTFB) by region and browser.
  • Bounded by: CORS → CORS; protocol choice → when each HTTP version matters.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: The Network panel shows the client users actually run. The timing breakdown splits each request into browser queueing, DNS, connect, TLS, waiting and download, and the Protocol column shows h1, h2 or h3. It catches what curl can't: the 6-connection limit on HTTP/1.1, CORS preflights, cookies and cache behaviour. "Copy as cURL" turns a failing row into a reproducible command.

Q · Mechanism — Why do requests queue in the browser on HTTP/1.1 but not HTTP/2? HTTP/1.1 carries one request at a time per connection, and browsers cap connections per host at 6, so the seventh request waits for one to free. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection, so there's no per-host queue for the same reason (only stream limits, typically 100).

Q · Trade-off — Lab measurement in DevTools or RUM? DevTools gives full detail for one session on your machine and network. RUM gives less detail but covers real users, devices and networks. DevTools to diagnose a mechanism; RUM to find out who's affected and how often.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Connections per host, HTTP/1.1 6 Chrome, Firefox, Safari default (as of Nov 2026): Chrome DevTools docs
Captured: requests 7–12 queued ~1,017 ms waiting for a free connection measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026
Captured: total for 12 requests ~2,023 ms 2 rounds of 6 measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "curl shows 1 s per call, so the page should take 1 s"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the calls run in parallel in the code.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: over HTTP/1.1 the browser sends only 6 at a time per host; the rest queue inside it.
    ↳ Think instead: read the Queueing bar, and serve over HTTP/2.
  • Don't debug with the cache enabled.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the default and reloads are faster.
    ↳ What goes wrong: (disk cache) rows hide the network entirely, so you time the wrong thing.
    ↳ Do instead: tick "Disable cache" while DevTools is open.
  • Not the same: Waiting (TTFB) vs server time
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the tooltip says "waiting for server response".
    ↳ Difference: it includes one round trip plus any proxy queueing, not just the handler.
    ↳ Think instead: TTFB − RTT ≈ server + queue; use Server-Timing to split it.
  • "An OPTIONS before every call is harmless"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's tiny and returns 204.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: each preflight costs a full round trip before the real request, doubling latency on cross-origin APIs.
    ↳ Think instead: Access-Control-Max-Age to cache it, or same-origin routing.
  • Shelf life: the connection limit and timing phases are durable; DevTools layout and labels move.

Connections

Path:curl masterybrowser Network paneldistributed tracing
  • Builds on where latency goes and HTTP/1.1 limits.
  • Owned elsewhere: CORS owns preflight rules; HTTP caching owns cache behaviour.
  • Breaks when combined with many parallel calls to one host over HTTP/1.1.
  • Bounded by being one session: RUM tells you if users see the same.

notes.title: Distributed Tracing — One traceparent That Survives Every Hop
notes.html:
References

W3C: Trace Context · OpenTelemetry: Context propagation · OpenTelemetry: Sampling · Envoy: Tracing

TL;DR

A trace follows one request across services. Each hop records a span (start, end, attributes) and passes context to the next hop in the traceparent header: version-traceid-parentid-flags.

  • The trace-id (32 hex) stays the same at every hop.
  • The parent-id (16 hex) changes to the current span at each hop.
  • Flags bit 0 says "sampled", so every hop makes the same keep-or-drop decision.

A trace breaks wherever a hop doesn't forward the header: a proxy, a queue or a thread pool that drops it. The result is two half-traces and a gap exactly where the latency is.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:edge creates 00-4bf9…4736-00f0…02b7-01proxy keeps trace-id, sets its own parent-idservice A reads it, starts a span, forwardsmessage queue carries it in message headersworker continues the same tracebackend stitches all spans by trace-id

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four traceparent fields? version (2 hex), trace-id (32), parent-id (16), flags (2).
Where does the sampling decision travel? In the flags: bit 0 = sampled.
Why do traces break at a proxy? It dropped or regenerated the header instead of continuing it.

The idea

A checkout request takes 4 seconds. The trace shows the API's span at 4 s and the payment service's span at 200 ms, and nothing between them. The 3.8 s is invisible because the request went through a message queue whose consumer started a new trace. The header was never copied into the message. Once the producer writes traceparent into message headers and the consumer continues from it, the gap shows up as a span: 3.7 s waiting in the queue.

The trade: one propagated header makes every hop's time visible in one picture, and you pay with instrumenting every hop (including proxies and queues), storage for spans, and a sampling policy that decides what you can see later.

How it works

Field Example Rule
version 00 current version
trace-id 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 same for the whole request, never all zeros
parent-id 00f067aa0ba902b7 the caller's span ID; each hop replaces it with its own
flags 01 bit 0 = sampled
Sampling Decided Keeps
head-based at the first hop, carried in flags a fixed share (e.g. 1 %), cheap, misses rare errors
tail-based after the trace ends, in a collector errors and slow traces, costs buffering every span

Evolution

Lineage:2010 Google's Dapper paper2012 Zipkin2015 Jaeger2019 OpenTelemetry (OpenTracing + OpenCensus)Feb 2020 W3C Trace Context Recommendation2023 OpenTelemetry tracing stable in major languages
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: W3C Trace Context Level 2 is in progress (a random-trace-id flag); proxies (Envoy, nginx's OTel module) and cloud LBs propagate traceparent.
  • What won't change: a hop that doesn't forward the header ends the trace.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026 (a Python 3.15 proxy in front of an upstream; the proxy continues the trace on /ok and drops the header on /ok?drop):

curl -H 'traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01' http://127.0.0.1:9200/ok
#   upstream saw traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-6c0c9232505584aa-01
#                                ↑ same trace-id                  ↑ new parent-id (the proxy's span)
curl -H 'traceparent: 00-4bf9…-01' 'http://127.0.0.1:9200/ok?drop'
#   upstream saw traceparent: -      ← header dropped: the upstream starts an unrelated trace

The default that bites: many proxies and HTTP clients forward only headers they know; nginx without the OpenTelemetry module forwards traceparent as an ordinary header but never adds its own span, so its time is invisible.

Measure it

  • See it: send a request with a fixed traceparent and grep each hop's logs for the trace-id; the first hop where it's missing is the break.
  • In production: share of traces with orphan spans (no parent), spans per trace by route, and trace-id in every log line for correlation.
  • Bounded by: sampling (what you didn't keep, you can't see) and metrics for the aggregate view.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A trace is spans from every hop linked by one trace-id. The W3C traceparent header carries version, trace-id, the caller's span ID and a sampled flag; each hop keeps the trace-id, sets its own span as the parent and forwards. Traces break where a hop doesn't propagate: proxies, queues, thread pools. I put the trace-id in logs too, and use tail sampling to keep errors and slow requests.

Q · Mechanism — How do spans from different services end up in one tree? Each span records its own span ID and its parent's span ID, read from the incoming traceparent. The backend groups spans by trace-id and links each to its parent, which rebuilds the call tree. Clock skew between hosts can make a child appear to start before its parent, which is why durations are measured on one host.

Q · Trade-off — Head-based or tail-based sampling? Head-based decides up front: cheap and consistent, but at 1 % you keep 1 % of the rare errors too. Tail-based decides after seeing the whole trace, so it keeps every error and slow request, but the collector must buffer all spans for a while. Head-based at low volume; tail-based when you need the rare bad traces.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
traceparent length 55 characters 2 + 32 + 16 + 2 hex, 3 dashes spec (as of Nov 2026): W3C Trace Context
Sampled flag bit 0 of flags 01 sampled, 00 not spec (as of Nov 2026): W3C Trace Context
Captured: trace-id across the proxy unchanged; parent-id replaced /ok measured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Instrumenting the services is enough"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the services are where the code is.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a proxy, queue or thread pool in between that drops the header splits the trace, and the gap is the slow part.
    ↳ Think instead: trace every hop, including message headers and async hand-offs.
  • Don't let each hop start a new trace when the header is missing without logging it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: starting fresh keeps tracing "working" everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: broken propagation becomes invisible; you get many short traces and no end-to-end view.
    ↳ Do instead: count root spans that should have had a parent.
  • Not the same: trace-id vs request-id
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are unique IDs per request in logs.
    ↳ Difference: a request-id is often per hop and ad hoc; a trace-id follows a standard header across every hop and links spans.
    ↳ Think instead: log the trace-id and retire private request-ids.
  • "1 % head sampling catches the problems"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it keeps storage small and looks statistically fine.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a 0.1 % error path is kept in only 1 % of cases, so you almost never have its trace.
    ↳ Think instead: tail sampling for errors and slow traces.
  • Shelf life: the header format is durable; SDKs, collectors and Level 2 additions move.

Connections

Path:browser Network paneldistributed tracingmetrics that matter
  • Builds on HTTP headers.
  • Owned elsewhere: tail latency owns what to do with slow spans.
  • Breaks when combined with proxies and queues that don't forward the header.
  • Bounded by sampling: you can only investigate traces you kept.

notes.title: The Metrics That Matter — RED at Every Hop, Plus What Runs Out
notes.html:
References

Google SRE book: Monitoring distributed systems (four golden signals) · Brendan Gregg: The USE method · Tom Wilkie: The RED method · Prometheus: Histograms and summaries

TL;DR

Two short lists cover almost every network-shaped incident:

  • RED at every hop (client, LB, proxy, service): Rate, Errors (split by status class and by who generated them), Duration as a histogram (p50, p99), never an average.
  • USE for what runs out: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors of the finite things: connections in pools, file descriptors, NAT ports, accept queues, bandwidth.

Two rules make them honest. Percentiles can't be averaged across instances; merge histograms instead. And each hop's view differs: the gap between the client's duration and the server's duration is network plus queueing.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:alert on the user-facing hop's REDcompare RED one hop downthe hop where errors or duration appear is the suspectcheck its USE (pool, fds, queue)saturated resource names the cause

Recall

Prompt Answer
RED and USE? Rate, Errors, Duration per hop; Utilisation, Saturation, Errors per resource.
Why not average the per-instance p99s? Percentiles don't combine; merge histograms and compute once.
Client duration minus server duration? Network plus queueing between them: the part no server dashboard shows.

The idea

Users complain about slowness. The service dashboard shows p99 at 80 ms, flat. The LB's dashboard shows p99 at 900 ms. The gap is between them: the LB waits for a free connection because the service's pool of 50 connections per instance is full (USE: saturation 100 %). The service measures from when it accepts a request, so it never sees the wait. Measuring the same request at two hops located the problem in one glance.

The trade: a small fixed set of metrics at every hop makes any incident locatable, and you pay with histogram storage, consistent labels across hops, and the discipline to instrument the boring finite resources nobody graphs until they run out.

How it works

Hop Rate Errors Duration Saturation to watch
client / SDK requests sent timeouts, resets, DNS failures full time incl. connect pool wait, in-flight count
load balancer requests 5xx it generated vs 5xx from targets target response time surge queue, spillover
proxy / mesh requests per route upstream_rq_5xx, retries, ejections upstream time active connections vs limit
service requests handled status codes handler time worker threads, db pool, fds

A model on Python 3.15 (24 Nov 2026): 10 instances × 10,000 requests, one instance sick on 5 % of requests.

Aggregate Value
per-instance p99s 74–79 ms, and 441 ms for the sick one
average of the 10 p99s 113 ms ✗
true fleet p99 (merged) 84 ms ✓
fleet mean 34 ms (hides the sick instance)

Evolution

Lineage:1990s SNMP counters2012 Brendan Gregg's USE method2015 Prometheus 1.0 and histograms2016 Google SRE book: four golden signals2018 the RED method2024 Prometheus native histograms and OpenTelemetry metrics stable
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: native (exponential) histograms give accurate percentiles without hand-picked buckets; exemplars link a metric point to a trace.
  • What won't change: percentiles don't average, and the caller's view differs from the server's.

On the wire

Merging histograms, in PromQL, with the default that bites:

# ✓ fleet p99: sum the buckets across instances, then take the quantile once
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
# ✗ avg(histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(...[5m])))   ← averages per-instance p99s: 113 ms vs a true 84 ms
# the default that bites: client libraries' default buckets top out at 10 s and are coarse
# around 100 ms–1 s, so a p99 between buckets is interpolated; set buckets around your SLO

Measure it

  • See it: the same request's duration at client, LB and service on one graph; the widening gap is where time goes.
  • In production: RED per hop per route, errors split by origin (LB-generated vs upstream), and USE for pools, fds, NAT ports and accept queues, each with its limit drawn on the graph.
  • Bounded by: aggregates hide individuals → tracing; tail behaviour → tail latency.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: At every hop I keep RED: rate, errors split by who generated them, and duration as a histogram. For every finite resource I keep USE: utilisation, saturation, errors for pools, file descriptors, ports and queues. I compare hops to locate the problem, since the gap between client and server duration is network plus queueing. And I merge histograms rather than averaging percentiles.

Q · Mechanism — Why is averaging p99s wrong? A percentile is a position in a sorted list, not a sum, so it doesn't combine linearly. One sick instance's huge p99 drags the average up, while its 1 % of traffic barely moves the fleet's true p99; in other cases the average understates it. Summing histogram buckets across instances and computing the quantile once gives the real answer.

Q · Trade-off — Histograms or summaries? Summaries compute quantiles in the client, exactly, but can't be merged across instances. Histograms count into buckets, can be summed across instances and time, but are approximate between bucket edges. Histograms for anything aggregated across a fleet; native histograms where available.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Average of per-instance p99s 113 ms vs 84 ms true derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Fleet mean in the same model 34 ms hides the sick instance derived; model run 24 Nov 2026
Prometheus default buckets 11, from 5 ms to 10 s client libraries default (as of Nov 2026): Prometheus client docs

Pitfalls

  • "Average latency tells us how users feel"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's one number and moves with load.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the mean hides the tail; in the model it showed 34 ms while one instance's p99 was 441 ms.
    ↳ Think instead: histograms, p50 and p99 per hop.
  • Don't average percentiles across instances or time.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: dashboards offer avg() over any series.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the number is meaningless: 113 ms in the model against a true 84 ms.
    ↳ Do instead: sum histogram buckets, then compute the quantile once.
  • Not the same: LB-generated 5xx vs upstream 5xx
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both count as 5xx on the LB's dashboard.
    ↳ Difference: a 502 or 504 made by the LB means it couldn't get an answer; a 500 passed through means the app answered with an error.
    ↳ Think instead: split errors by origin (ALB has separate metrics for each).
  • "CPU and memory are the resources to watch"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every dashboard template starts with them.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: network services usually run out of connections, fds, ports or queue slots first, at low CPU.
    ↳ Think instead: USE on every finite pool, with the limit drawn on the graph.
  • Shelf life: RED, USE and the percentile rule are durable; histogram formats and tools move.

  • Owned elsewhere: capacity planning owns the ceilings' limits.
  • Breaks when combined with dashboards that average percentiles.
  • Bounded by aggregation: metrics locate a problem, traces explain one request.

notes.title: Triage Playbooks — Symptom → Three Checks → Owner
notes.html:
References

RFC 9110 §15.6: Server error 5xx · nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module · AWS: Troubleshoot your Application Load Balancer · Envoy: Access log response flags

TL;DR

A playbook maps a symptom to two or three checks, ordered so each one rules out the most suspects, and ends at an owner. Five symptoms cover most network incidents:

  • 502 / 503 / 504: the proxy made them. 502 = the upstream refused, reset or sent garbage; 503 = no healthy upstream; 504 = the upstream was slower than the proxy's timeout.
  • Slow for some users: segment first (region, client version, new vs reused connection), then measure.
  • Works in curl, fails in the browser: CORS preflight, cookies, CSP or HTTP/3: things curl doesn't send.
  • Streaming stalls: a buffering hop (proxy buffering, a CDN) or an idle timeout.
  • Intermittent resets: idle-timeout mismatch between hops, or a leak (CLOSE_WAIT).

Read the code as an accusation of the hop that generated it, and check that hop's logs first.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request
Flow:symptomwho generated it? (LB log, server header, response flags)that hop's log for the upstream status and timingone targeted check (curl --resolve, ss, dig)owner namedmitigate first, fix second

Recall

Prompt Answer
Who emits 502, 503 and 504? The proxy or LB, not the app. Refused or reset · no healthy upstream · upstream slower than the proxy's timeout.
"Slow for some users": first move? Segment by region, client, and new vs reused connection before measuring.
"Works in curl, not the browser": suspects? CORS preflight, cookies, CSP, HTTP/3.
Streaming arrives all at once at the end? A hop buffering the response: proxy buffering or a CDN.
Resets at round intervals (60 s, 350 s)? An idle timeout on some hop shorter than the one behind it.
Draw by hand: the 5xx tree A hexagon "who generated it?"; LB branch splits into 502 (refused, reset), 503 (none healthy), 504 (too slow); app branch: 500 → app logs.

The idea

At 2 a.m. the alert says "5xx rate 8 %". A team without a playbook opens the app's logs, finds no errors, and concludes it's "the network". A team with one first asks which hop generated the errors. The ALB metrics show HTTPCode_ELB_504_Count rising and HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count flat: the LB is giving up, the app isn't failing. The LB's target_processing_time sits at exactly 60 s for those requests, its idle timeout. One query to the database shows a lock. Fifteen minutes, not two hours.

The playbook's value isn't knowledge; it's the order. Each check cuts the suspect list in half, so nobody spends an hour on the hop that was never involved.

The trade: written playbooks turn incidents into a short, repeatable search that anyone on call can run, and you pay with maintaining them as the architecture changes, and with logs at every hop that record who generated each response and how long the upstream took.

How it works

The 5xx tree: who made it decides where to look.

The other four playbooks:

Symptom Check 1 Check 2 Check 3 Usual owner
slow for some users segment: region, ISP, client version new vs reused connections (time_connect > 0?) DNS answer and route per region edge or CDN config, a region's path
works in curl, not browser DevTools: is there an OPTIONS row? cookies and SameSite CSP or mixed-content errors in console API's CORS config, front end
streaming stalls curl -N direct vs through each hop X-Accel-Buffering, proxy_buffering idle timeouts on each hop vs heartbeat interval proxy or CDN config

Evolution

Lineage:1990s runbooks for NOC operators2003 Google SRE playbooks2016 SRE book: "be prepared, not heroic"2018 Envoy response flags (UF, UT, UH) say which failure a proxy saw2020s runbooks linked from alerts, and LLM assistants that read logs and suggest the next check
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026).
  • Changed recently: proxies log a failure reason with every 5xx (Envoy response flags, ALB error_reason); AI on-call assistants draft first checks from runbooks.
  • What won't change: the hop that generated the response knows why; ask it first.

On the wire

Captured on localhost, 24 Nov 2026: a Python 3.15 reverse proxy standing in for nginx (nginx isn't installed on this machine), with a 1 s upstream timeout. The mapping is the same as nginx's.

for p in /ok /down /drain /slow; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "GET $p → %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n" http://127.0.0.1:9200$p; done
# GET /ok → 200 in 0.002502s
# GET /down → 502 in 0.000776s     ← nothing listening upstream: refused, immediately
# GET /drain → 503 in 0.000501s    ← no upstream in the pool at all
# GET /slow → 504 in 1.002029s     ← upstream alive, needed 2 s; the proxy gave up at its 1 s

The default that bites: nginx's proxy_read_timeout is 60 s and the ALB's idle timeout is 60 s, so a 504 at exactly 60 s points at one of those timers, not at a dead upstream.

Break it: the core of the proxy above (Python 3.15, run 24 Nov 2026):

try:
    c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", port, timeout=1.0)
    c.request("GET", path); r = c.getresponse(); reply(r.status)
except ConnectionRefusedError:            reply(502)   # upstream refused or reset
except (TimeoutError, socket.timeout):    reply(504)   # upstream slower than OUR timeout
# look for: the upstream on /slow returned 200 after 2 s; its own log shows success
# naive belief predicts: a 504 means the upstream is down or broken

Run: /slow came back 504 in 1.002 s while the upstream completed its 200 a second later. The upstream was healthy; the proxy's timeout was shorter than the upstream's work. The fix is either a faster upstream or a deliberate timeout budget (timeout hierarchy), not restarting the upstream.

Measure it

  • See it: the proxy's access log with upstream status and upstream time on every line (nginx $upstream_status $upstream_response_time, Envoy %RESPONSE_FLAGS%).
  • In production: 5xx split by origin (ALB HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count vs HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count), upstream time histograms that show a wall at the timeout, and each alert linked to its playbook.
  • Bounded by: which logs exist: a hop that doesn't log upstream status and time can't be triaged → metrics that matter.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: I first ask which hop generated the symptom. 502, 503 and 504 come from the proxy: 502 means the upstream refused or reset, 503 none was healthy, 504 it was slower than the proxy's timeout, often a dependency underneath. Then that hop's log for upstream status and timing, then one targeted check. "Some users slow" starts with segmenting; "curl works, browser fails" with CORS and cookies; stalls with buffering hops; resets with idle-timeout order.

Q · Mechanism — Why does the upstream's log show success for a request the user saw as a 504? The proxy gave up at its timeout and returned 504 to the client, but the upstream kept working and eventually wrote a 200 to a connection nobody was reading. Each hop logs its own view. That's why the proxy's upstream time, sitting exactly at the timeout, is the evidence, and the upstream's success is not a contradiction.

Q · Trade-off — Mitigate first, or find the root cause first? Mitigation (roll back, shift traffic, shed load) restores users in minutes but can destroy evidence, such as a restarted process with its leaked sockets gone. Root cause first keeps evidence but extends the outage. Mitigate first, after grabbing the cheap evidence: one ss -s, a heap or thread dump, the last log lines.

Q · Failure — 502s only during deploys. What's going on? Old instances are killed while the LB still sends them requests, or they close kept-alive connections the LB is about to reuse. Check: connection draining and deregistration delay on the LB, a preStop sleep so endpoints update before the process exits, and the app's keep-alive timeout longer than the LB's idle timeout. See rollouts and connection handling.

Q · Design — Make 5xx incidents triageable by anyone on call.

  • Every hop logs upstream address, upstream status, upstream time and a failure reason.
  • Metrics split by origin: LB-generated vs target-generated.
  • Trace-id in every log line, so one request can be followed across hops.
  • Alerts link a playbook whose first line is "which hop generated it?"
  • Timeouts are written down per hop, so a wall at 60 s is recognisable at once.

Compare

Code Generated by Upstream state First look Common cause
500 the app answered, with an error app logs exception
502 proxy refused, reset, or invalid response is the process up, listening on that port? crash, deploy, keep-alive race
503 proxy (or app shedding) none healthy, or shedding health checks, pool size, Retry-After failing checks, scaled to zero
504 proxy alive but slower than the proxy's timeout upstream time vs timeout slow dependency, lock, cold start

Pitfalls

  • "A 504 means the upstream is down"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "gateway timeout" sounds like the server is gone.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the upstream was usually alive and slower than the proxy's timer; in the capture it finished its 200 after the 504 was sent.
    ↳ Think instead: 504 = slower than the proxy's timeout; look at what the upstream was waiting on.
  • Don't start in the app's logs for a 502, 503 or 504.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the app is what you own and know best.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the app never saw those requests or didn't fail them, so you find nothing and call it "the network".
    ↳ Do instead: the proxy's log first: upstream status, time and failure reason.
  • Not the same: 502 vs 503
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean the proxy couldn't get a good response.
    ↳ Difference: 502 means it tried an upstream that refused, reset or sent garbage; 503 means it had none to try, or something is shedding.
    ↳ Think instead: 502: is it running? 503: is it in the pool?
  • "Restart it" as the first step
    ↳ Why it's tempting: restarts often make the symptom go away.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it destroys the evidence (leaked sockets, thread state) and the problem returns.
    ↳ Think instead: grab cheap evidence (ss -s, a thread dump), then mitigate.
  • Don't measure "slow for some users" as one average.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one fleet-wide graph is the quickest thing to open.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the affected 5 % disappear in the mean, so the graph looks normal.
    ↳ Do instead: segment by region, client and connection reuse before measuring.
  • Shelf life: the 5xx meanings and the order of checks are durable; log fields and metric names move.

Connections

  • Owned elsewhere: CORS owns browser-only failures; server-sent events owns streaming through buffering proxies.
  • Breaks when combined with hops that don't log upstream status and time.
  • Bounded by the logs you have: a playbook can only ask questions some hop records.
